meta.descriptionEn: On 22 October 2008, India launched its first probe to the Moon on a budget of 386 crore rupees. Within weeks, a small impact probe slammed into the lunar south pole, near Shackleton crater. The orbiter mapped the Moon, overheated, lost its star tracker, and then, on 28 August 2009, went silent after just 312 days. Many feared it was gone for good. Then, in 2016, NASA radar found it still circling the Moon. But the biggest twist came from its instruments: signs of water in lunar soil. How did a failing spacecraft change what we know about the Moon? And who really saw the water first? Watch the full story.
meta.descriptionUr: 22 October 2008 ko India ne apna pehla Moon mission Chandrayaan-1 launch kiya. Sirf 312 din baad is se rabta toot gaya aur sab ne socha ke mission khatam ho gaya. Lekin 2016 mein NASA ke radar ne ise dobara Chand ke orbit mein dhoond nikala. Is ke instruments ne Chand par paani ke nishan bhi dikhaye. Yeh kahani hai ek chhote se probe ki jis ne badi cheezein badal di. Paani sab se pehle kis ne dekha? Video akhir tak dekhein.

articleEn: On the night of 28 August 2009, at around 20:00 UTC, ISRO suddenly lost contact with its first lunar probe, Chandrayaan-1. The mission was meant to last two years, but the spacecraft worked for only 312 days, less than half of the planned time.

ISRO Chairman G. Madhavan Nair said that excessive radiation had caused the power-supply units controlling both computer systems to fail. Later information tells a different story, suggesting the power supply failed because of overheating. So what was the real cause?

This story is about more than a broken link. It is about a spacecraft that changed how people think about the Moon. Chandrayaan-1 discovered widespread water molecules in lunar soil, and according to a scientists' review, the mission achieved 95 percent of its primary objectives. The spacecraft was expected to stay in orbit for roughly another 1,000 days and strike the Moon's surface in late 2012.

Then came another surprise. In 2016, NASA used ground-based radar to find the silent spacecraft again in orbit around the Moon. How was a silent probe identified about seven years later? We will answer that question, but first, how did this mission begin, and what dream lay behind it?

articleEn: Like every great mission, Chandrayaan-1 began as an idea. It was first raised in 1999 at a meeting of the Indian Academy of Sciences, with the proposal that India send its own scientific mission to the Moon. At that point it was only an idea, and much work lay ahead. In 2000, the Astronautical Society of India began planning to turn it into reality. Soon after, ISRO formed the National Lunar Mission Task Force, which concluded that ISRO had the technical expertise to take an Indian mission to the Moon. The dream now began to look possible.

In April 2003, more than 100 Indian scientists gathered in one place, including experts in planetary science, physics, chemistry, astronomy, engineering and communication sciences. They debated the Task Force's recommendation and approved it: India should send its own probe to the Moon. Six months later, in November 2003, the Vajpayee government formally approved the mission, and then Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee announced the Chandrayaan-1 project.

ISRO was not a new agency. Its roots went back decades to 1962, when it began as INCOSPAR, created by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on the recommendation of scientist Vikram Sarabhai. It was renamed ISRO in 1969. India's first satellite, Aryabhata, reached orbit on a Soviet rocket in 1975. In 1980, ISRO launched the RS-1 satellite on its own SLV-3, making India the seventh country to carry out orbital launches. In the 1990s came the PSLV, a major boost for the Indian space programme.

In 1969, Vikram Sarabhai had said that the goal was not to compete with wealthy nations in lunar exploration, but to apply advanced technologies to India's real problems. Now a big test lay ahead: Chandrayaan-1 was to orbit the Moon using India's own technology and launch vehicle. The estimated cost was ₹386 crore, about 88.73 million US dollars, and the plan was to survey the lunar surface for two years.

The survey aimed to produce a complete map of the Moon's chemical composition and a three-dimensional topography. The polar regions were of special interest because water ice might exist there. The plan was ready, but which instruments could fit into such a small spacecraft, and how would they read the Moon?

articleEn: Chandrayaan-1 did not look like a big machine. It was a cuboid of about 1.5 metres, weighing 1,380 kg at launch, 675 kg after reaching lunar orbit, and only 523 kg after releasing its impactor. A whole mission fitted into very little mass.

For power it had a single solar panel measuring 2.15 by 1.8 metres, producing at most 750 W. The energy was stored in a 36 Ampere-hour lithium-ion battery so the spacecraft could keep running during eclipses. The engine that carried it to the Moon was a 440 Newton unit, supported by eight small 22 Newton thrusters and two tanks of fuel and oxidizer. To control its orientation it had two star sensors, gyros and four reaction wheels. Remember this, because a sensor failure would later become an important turning point.

The spacecraft had three main goals. The first was a three-dimensional atlas of the Moon covering both near and far sides, with a spatial and altitude resolution of 5 to 10 metres. The second was chemical and mineralogical mapping of the entire surface. The third and most intriguing was to search the polar regions for surface or subsurface water ice, especially in permanently shadowed areas.

To do this, the spacecraft carried 11 instruments, five Indian and six from other countries and institutions, with a total scientific payload of 90 kg. The Indian instruments included the Terrain Mapping Camera, or TMC, which took black-and-white stereo images at 5 metre resolution with a 40 km swath. The Hyper Spectral Imager, HySI, mapped minerals in the 400 to 900 nanometre band. The Lunar Laser Ranging Instrument, LLRI, measured surface height using laser pulses. The HEX spectrometer measured 30 to 200 keV, and the Moon Impact Probe was the fifth Indian instrument, which would become a story of its own.

Among the foreign instruments, C1XS was an X-ray spectrometer built with Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, ESA and ISRO. ESA's SARA measured mineral composition using low-energy neutral atoms, while SIR-2 was a near-infrared spectrometer built by several institutions including the Max Planck Institute. NASA contributed two instruments: the Moon Mineralogy Mapper, M3, from Brown University and JPL, and Mini-SAR, a radar to search for polar ice. Finally, the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences provided RADOM-7, which measured the radiation environment around the Moon.

All the foreign instruments were carried free of charge. When the International Lunar Exploration Working Group gave the mission an award, it called it the most international lunar payload to date, involving 20 countries. Now only the launch remained.

articleEn: On the morning of 22 October 2008, the PSLV-C11 rocket stood on the launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, at 00:52 UTC. It was a four-stage rocket 44.4 metres tall, with Chandrayaan-1, India's first lunar probe, on top. The rocket placed it in a geostationary transfer orbit, with a farthest point of 22,860 kilometres and a nearest point of 255 kilometres.

But Chandrayaan-1 did not go straight to the Moon. It went through a series of manoeuvres that raised its orbit around the Earth over about 21 days. The first burn took place on 23 October at 03:30 UTC. The 440 Newton liquid engine ran for about 18 minutes, raising the apogee to 37,900 kilometres, and one orbit of the Earth took about 11 hours. The second burn, on 25 October, raised the apogee to 74,715 kilometres. It was the first time an Indian spacecraft had gone beyond the 36,000 kilometre geostationary orbit, and it had now travelled more than twice that distance.

The third burn, on 26 October, lasted about nine and a half minutes and raised the apogee to 164,600 kilometres, with one orbit taking about 73 hours. The fourth burn, on 29 October, lasted only about three minutes and raised the apogee to 267,000 kilometres, more than half the way to the Moon. The fifth and final burn took place on 3 November at 23:26 UTC. The engine ran for only two and a half minutes, and Chandrayaan-1 entered the Lunar Transfer Trajectory.

Then came 8 November 2008. At 11:21 UTC, Chandrayaan-1 was passing just 500 kilometres from the Moon, and the engine fired again for lunar orbit insertion. It ran for 817 seconds, about 13.5 minutes. Would the spacecraft stay in orbit around the Moon? The answer came quickly: Chandrayaan-1 was now in an elliptical orbit passing over the lunar polar regions, with a farthest point of 7,502 kilometres and a nearest point of 504 kilometres. With this success India became the fifth country to put a vehicle around the Moon. The orbital period was then estimated at about 11 hours.

The work was not finished. On 9 November the first orbit reduction ran the engine for about 57 seconds and lowered the nearest point to 200 kilometres. On 10 November the second reduction brought the orbit to 255 by 187 kilometres, with one orbit taking two hours 16 minutes. On 11 November the third reduction ran the engine for 31 seconds and lowered the low point to 101 kilometres.

On 12 November 2008, Chandrayaan-1 reached its mission polar orbit, 100 kilometres above the lunar surface, completing one orbit in about two hours. That same day two instruments, the Terrain Mapping Camera and RADOM, were switched on, and the TMC photographed both Earth and the Moon. But another big moment was near.

articleEn: Chandrayaan-1 was now in a 100 kilometre polar orbit, but it carried a small passenger that had to travel to the Moon's surface alone: the Moon Impact Probe, or MIP. Former president Abdul Kalam had suggested that since the orbiter was already near the Moon, a probe would add to the mission's importance. MIP had three aims: to demonstrate the technology of reaching a specific location, to qualify technologies for future soft landings, and to observe from close range before impact. Its body was an aluminium-honeycomb sandwich structure, and on its four vertical sides were four oval plates bearing the Indian flag, each 120 by 180 millimetres.

The moment came on 14 November 2008. At 14:36 UTC, MIP separated from Chandrayaan-1, released from the orbiter by a ball lock separation system. The sources differ here: one gives the separation time as 14:30 UTC, and one gives the date as 18 November. Most sources agree on 14 November and 14:36 UTC. The orbit height also varies, with one source calling it a 100 kilometre circular polar orbit and another 102 kilometres.

After separation, spin-up rockets fired first to keep the probe stable. Then a retro rocket pushed it out of orbit toward the lunar surface. During this descent of about 25 minutes, the probe kept sending data, which first went to the orbiter and was then relayed to Earth. One source puts the free fall at about thirty minutes, while others say 25 minutes, so it is best treated as an estimate.

The video imaging system, an analog CCD camera, took close-up pictures of the surface, which later helped identify the impact site. The third instrument was CHACE, a quadrupole mass spectrometer, whose job was to measure trace elements in the lunar atmosphere during descent. CHACE took 650 mass spectra readings on the trip. ISRO later said these contained evidence of water, but that story comes later.

At 15:01 UTC the probe touched the Moon's surface at a speed of 1.69 kilometres per second, about 6,100 kilometres per hour. The site was near the edge of Shackleton crater, at the Moon's south pole. With this, ISRO became the fifth national space agency to reach the lunar surface, after the Soviet Union in 1959, America in 1962, Japan in 1993 and ESA member countries in 2006.

The site was named Jawahar Sthal in India, after the country's first prime minister, and one source also calls it Jawahar Point. The name was proposed by Abdul Kalam, and the impact took place on Nehru's birthday. The initial estimate was 89.76 degrees south. Later, MIP camera images were matched against an LROC mosaic, and the site was placed on the slope of the ridge between Shackleton and De Gerlache, near 89.55 degrees south.

chapters.covers: Temperature rose to 50 °C on 25 November 2008; instruments switched off and spacecraft rotated; later blamed on DC-DC converters with poor thermal regulation; orbit raised from 100 km to 200 km on 19 May 2009 to reduce heat; star tracker failure after nine months, backup with Sun sensor and gyroscopes; failed bistatic radar experiment on 21 August 2009 because the radar was not pointed at the Moon.

articleEn: Now the story hits a problem. Work around the Moon had begun, but the spacecraft had a silent enemy: heat. On 25 November 2008, ISRO announced that Chandrayaan-1's temperature had risen above normal to 50 degrees centigrade. Scientists said lunar orbit was hotter than expected. At first it was thought that solar radiation and infrared heat reflected from the Moon were raising the temperature. The team turned the spacecraft by about 20 degrees and switched off some instruments, which brought the temperature down by about 10 degrees. On 27 November ISRO said the spacecraft was running at normal temperature.

But later reports recorded heat above normal again. So by January 2009, when lunar orbit conditions were supposed to be stable, it was decided to run only one instrument at a time. The real cause turned out to be different: the heat was linked to a batch of DC-DC converters with weak thermal regulation. Even so, the mission moved forward. On 29 January 2009, scientists from India, Europe and America reviewed the results after 100 days. On 25 March 2009, the TMC sent images of the whole Earth for the first time, showing parts of Asia, Africa and Australia, with India in the middle.

On 19 May 2009, the orbit was raised from 100 to 200 kilometres. The stated purpose was to study orbit perturbations and the Moon's gravitational field. It later emerged that the real reason was to keep the spacecraft cooler. The temperature at 100 kilometres had been expected to be around 75 degrees, but it turned out higher. So was heat the only problem? No.

Another vital part of the spacecraft began to fail: the star tracker, a device for determining orientation, or attitude. It failed in orbit after working for about nine months. The team then adopted a backup method, determining orientation using a two-axis Sun sensor and a bearing taken from an Earth station, and then using that to update the three-axis gyroscopes, which kept operations going. A second fault was detected on 16 May and was linked to stronger solar radiation.

Then came 21 August 2009. That day Chandrayaan-1 and NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter tried a bistatic radar experiment using their Mini-SAR radars, aiming to test for water ice on the lunar surface. The attempt failed because Chandrayaan-1's radar was not pointed at the Moon at the time. That experiment failed, but the rest of Mini-SAR's work continued, and it imaged many permanently shadowed regions at both poles.

ISRO also announced in January 2009 that mapping of the Apollo landing sites was complete. Six sites were mapped, including Apollo 15 and Apollo 17. Despite its problems, the spacecraft was working. But heat, faulty sensors and radiation were building up pressure. Could Chandrayaan-1 withstand more?

articleEn: At around 20:00 UTC on 28 August 2009, contact with Chandrayaan-1 was suddenly lost. The mission was then 312 days old, though it had been planned for two years. ISRO Chairman G. Madhavan Nair said excessive radiation had caused the power-supply units controlling both computer systems to fail. But information that emerged later says something different: according to it, the power supply provided by MDI failed because of overheating. The sources disagree, with radiation on one side and heat on the other. According to a member of the science advisory board, it is hard to determine the real cause. The spacecraft was supposed to stay in orbit for about another 1,000 days and hit the Moon's surface in late 2012.

But the story does not end there. A scientists' review called the mission a success, because 95 percent of its primary objectives had been completed. What did it achieve? The spacecraft completed 3,000 orbits and obtained 70,000 images of the lunar surface, a record compared with many lunar missions of other countries. Some images had a resolution of up to 5 metres, while many images from other missions had 100 metre resolution. The Moon Mineralogy Mapper, M3, mapped more than 95 percent of the surface, and TMC and HySI covered about 70 percent. However, M3 made this coverage in its low-resolution Global mode; in the high-resolution Target mode it saw only a small portion. The six Apollo landing sites were also mapped.

Now to the biggest discovery: water on the Moon. On 24 September 2009, Science magazine reported that M3 had detected water. M3 saw absorption features near 2.8 to 3.0 μm on the lunar surface. In silicate bodies, such features are usually linked to hydroxyl or water-bearing materials. The absorption was especially strong at cold, high latitudes. According to scientists, this suggests that the formation of OH and H2O is still ongoing.

The next day, 25 September 2009, ISRO announced that the Moon Impact Probe had detected water during its descent before impact. According to ISRO, this discovery came before NASA's M3 finding, but it was not announced until NASA had confirmed. After analysing the readings, ISRO confirmed the water. MIP's CHACE instrument had recorded evidence of water in its 650 mass spectra readings during the descent.

Then in 2018, M3's full data was reanalysed. It gave the clearest evidence yet of water in shadowed craters near the poles. The detailed analysis found surface water ice concentrations of 2 to 30 percent at several places above 70 degrees latitude.

Mini-SAR data also turned out to be interesting. In March 2010 it was reported that more than 40 dark craters had been found near the north pole, with an estimated 600 million tonnes of water-ice. But scientists also urged caution. That signature would require the ice to be relatively pure and at least a few metres thick, yet the observations do not match thick, nearly pure layers. However, ice pieces smaller than about 10 centimetres could be mixed into the regolith. So is Moon water such a simple matter? The most surprising twist was still to come.

articleEn: The story's most surprising twist came on 2 July 2016. NASA used ground-based radar systems and found Chandrayaan-1 again in lunar orbit, about seven years after it went silent. Repeated observations over the next three months established its orbit accurately. Its altitude was found to vary between 150 and 270 kilometres every two years. The silent probe had been quietly circling the Moon. It had been expected to hit the Moon in late 2012, but in 2016 it turned out to still be in orbit.

Now let us see what the mission left behind. M3 data confirmed the magma ocean hypothesis, meaning the Moon was once entirely molten. M3 also found a strange rock in the inner western ring of the Moscoviense Basin. It was rich in Mg-spinel, with less than 5 percent pyroxene or olivine. According to the report, this spinel does not fit easily into current lunar-crustal evolution models, so a new question was raised.

Chandrayaan-1 also saw a lunar rille formed by an ancient lava flow. It had an uncollapsed section, hinting at a lava tube. It is about 2 kilometres long and 360 metres wide, and was found near the equator. According to A. S. Arya, it could be a possible site for human settlement. Mini-SAR data showed traces of past tectonic activity, and researchers think these faults may result from past internal activity and meteorite impacts.

The mission also earned recognition. AIAA chose it for its SPACE 2009 awards, and the National Space Society gave it the 2009 Space Pioneer Award. The data was also opened to the public: the first part was to be released by the end of 2010 and the second by mid-2011, including images and chemical and mineral mapping.

What happened next? Chandrayaan-2 launched on 22 July 2019, with an orbiter, the Vikram lander and the Pragyan rover. The lander crashed because of a last-minute glitch in its landing guidance software, but the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter remained operational as of September 2023. Then Chandrayaan-3 launched on 14 July 2023 and made a successful soft landing on the Moon on 23 August 2023. So the journey went on.

Is the question of Moon water settled? According to one report, scientists are now confident, but questions remain about the Mini-SAR results and the form of the ice. Another lesson of this journey is thermal design. Reports of poor thermal regulation in the DC-DC converters and overheating in the power supply are linked to the mission's problems. More heat than expected was found in the 100 km orbit, so the team had to raise the orbit to 200 km. Estimating temperature is vital in space missions.

One last question: Chandrayaan-1 went apparently silent, but is its data still producing new discoveries today? The 2018 reanalysis suggests it is. If you liked this story, like the video, subscribe to the channel, and tell us in the comments where you think the Moon's water came from.

shorts.titleEn: The Night India's Moon Probe Went Silent
shorts.text: کیا ایک spacecraft بغیر کسی وارننگ کے اچانک خاموش ہو سکتا ہے؟ 28 August 2009 کی رات تقریباً 20:00 UTC پر ISRO کا اپنے پہلے lunar probe، Chandrayaan-1 سے رابطہ اچانک ٹوٹ گیا۔ یہ mission دو سال چلنا تھا۔ لیکن spacecraft صرف 312 دن کام کر سکا۔ ISRO کے Chairman G. Madhavan Nair نے کہا کہ بہت زیادہ radiation کی وجہ سے دونوں computer systems کو کنٹرول کرنے والی power-supply units فیل ہو گئیں۔ مگر بعد میں آنے والی معلومات کچھ اور بتاتی ہیں۔ ان کے مطابق MDI کی فراہم کردہ power supply overheating کی وجہ سے خراب ہوئی تھی۔ یعنی sources میں اختلاف ہے۔ مگر کیا یہ خاموش probe واقعی ختم ہو چکا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya aik spacecraft baghair kisi warning ke achanak khamosh ho sakta hai? 28 August 2009 ki raat taqreeban 20:00 UTC par ISRO ka apne pehle lunar probe, Chandrayaan-1 se rabta achanak toot gaya. Yeh mission do saal chalna tha. Lekin spacecraft sirf 312 din kaam kar saka. ISRO ke Chairman G. Madhavan Nair ne kaha ke bohat zyada radiation ki wajah se dono computer systems ko control karne wali power-supply units fail ho gayin. Magar baad mein aane wali maloomat kuch aur batati hain. Un ke mutabiq MDI ki faraham kardah power supply overheating ki wajah se kharab hui thi. Yaani sources mein ikhtilaf hai. Magar kya yeh khamosh probe waqai khatam ho chuka tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: On 28 August 2009, ISRO lost contact with Chandrayaan-1 after 312 days. Sources disagree on whether radiation or overheating was the cause.

shorts.titleEn: The 25-Minute Fall of India's Moon Impact Probe
shorts.text: ایک چھوٹا سا probe، اور اس کا سفر صرف 25 منٹ کا تھا۔ 14 November 2008 کو Chandrayaan-1 تقریباً 100 km اونچائی پر Moon کے polar orbit میں تھا۔ 14:36 UTC پر Moon Impact Probe اس سے الگ ہوا۔ اس پر تین instruments تھے: Radar Altimeter، Video Imaging System اور CHACE mass spectrometer۔ اترتے وقت یہ مسلسل معلومات orbiter کو بھیجتا رہا، اور orbiter وہ Earth تک پہنچاتا رہا۔ پھر 15:01 UTC پر یہ Shackleton Crater کے قریب جا ٹکرایا۔ اس کی رفتار 1.69 km فی second تھی، یعنی تقریباً 6,100 km فی hour۔ یوں ISRO Moon کی surface تک پہنچنے والا پانچواں national space agency بنا۔ مگر impact سے ذرا پہلے probe نے کیا ڈھونڈ لیا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Aik chhota sa probe, aur is ka safar sirf 25 minute ka tha. 14 November 2008 ko Chandrayaan-1 taqreeban 100 km unchai par Moon ke polar orbit mein tha. 14:36 UTC par Moon Impact Probe is se alag hua. Is par teen instruments thay: Radar Altimeter, Video Imaging System aur CHACE mass spectrometer. Utarte waqt yeh musalsal maloomat orbiter ko bhejta raha, aur orbiter woh Earth tak pohanchata raha. Phir 15:01 UTC par yeh Shackleton Crater ke qareeb ja takraya. Is ki raftar 1.69 km fi second thi, yaani taqreeban 6,100 km fi hour. Yun ISRO Moon ki surface tak pohanchne wala panchwan national space agency bana. Magar impact se zara pehle probe ne kya dhoond liya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: On 14 November 2008, India's Moon Impact Probe separated from Chandrayaan-1 and hit near Shackleton Crater after about 25 minutes.

shorts.roman: Kya koi spacecraft khatam hone ke taqreeban saat saal baad dobara mil sakta hai? Chandrayaan-1 ke saath aisa hi hua. 28 August 2009 ko is se rabta toot gaya tha. Tawaqqo thi ke yeh 2012 ke aakhir mein Moon ki surface se takra jaye ga. Phir aaya 2 July 2016. NASA ne ground-based radar systems istemal kiye aur Chandrayaan-1 ko lunar orbit mein dobara dhoond nikala. Agle teen mahinon mein baar baar observations hui, jin se is ka orbit bilkul durust maloom ho gaya. Pata chala ke har do saal mein is ki altitude 150 se 270 km ke darmiyan badalti rehti hai. Lekin jate jate yeh mission apne peechay kya chhor gaya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: In July 2016, NASA used ground-based radar to relocate Chandrayaan-1 in lunar orbit almost seven years after it went silent.
